item.title: What If Your Arctic Adventure Had No Roads?
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
On Andørja, one of Northern Europe’s most mountainous islands, Norrøna is creating a new kind of Arctic basecamp. Opening in June 2027, the Norrøna Lodge at Andørja will place travelers on one of Norway’s most remote coastlines, where 20 peaks rise more than 1,000 meters from the fjords and many are accessible only from the water.

The 15-cabin lodge will accommodate up to 30 guests and was designed to preserve the landscape rather than overpower it. Built around a former basking shark research center, the property uses timber construction, elevated structures and boardwalks, with no road access on site. Guests will arrive by boat, weather permitting, and stays will include guiding, dining, transportation and recovery. Depending on the season, experiences range from backcountry skiing, hiking, climbing and trail running beneath the midnight sun to northern lights excursions, snowshoeing and fishing. Local guides will also introduce guests to Andørja’s fishing traditions and communities, while wood-fired saunas, outdoor hot tubs and fjord dips provide a slower counterpoint to the adventure.

The Curated Take: Norrøna is making an interesting leap from creating equipment for outdoor exploration to creating the destinations themselves. At Andørja, that philosophy is particularly compelling because the lodge is designed to make the landscape more accessible without turning it into a conventional resort. With locally sourced Arctic ingredients such as king crab, sea urchin, berries and wild herbs complementing the experience, this is adventure travel built around immersion rather than simply activity. The lodge will also serve as the first destination in Norrøna’s planned Arctic Voyage, a growing network intended to connect some of Norway’s most untouched coastline.

item.title: What If the Road Became the Destination?
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
The original Grand Tour was as much about how travelers experienced Europe as where they went. Anantara Hotels & Resorts and Alfa Romeo are bringing that idea into the present with the Anantara Grand Tour of Europe, pairing scenic driving routes, Italian craftsmanship and stays at luxury hotels with a slower approach to travel.

The first journey, the Dolce Vita Tour, traces a particularly evocative route through Italy, beginning at Anantara Palazzo Naiadi Rome Hotel and winding through the Castelli Romani and along the coast to Sperlonga before continuing to Ravello and the Amalfi Coast. Guests travel in Alfa Romeo models ranging from the classic Giulietta to the contemporary Giulia and Stelvio, with opportunities for more performance-oriented Quadrifoglio models. Along the way, the itinerary layers in seaside lunches, family-run vineyard tastings and leisurely walks beneath Positano’s pastel-colored skyline before concluding at Anantara Convento di Amalfi Grand Hotel.

The Curated Take: The appeal here is less about checking off Italian landmarks than about reclaiming the pleasure of the journey between them. By putting the road, the automobile, local food and hospitality on equal footing with the destination, Anantara and Alfa Romeo offer a contemporary interpretation of slow travel with a distinctly European sense of style. Future itineraries will extend the concept to the French Riviera, Málaga to Marbella, Dublin to Amsterdam and a route through Europe’s Imperial Capitals.

The Dolce Vita Tour is now available to book through Anantara’s European Grand Tour collection.

item.title: What If Your Winter Holiday Looked Nothing Like Winter?
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
While much of the world heads toward snow and traditional Christmas markets, Lombok offers a very different way to celebrate the holiday season. On the island’s north coast, The Sira, a Luxury Collection Resort & Spa is drawing on Sasak heritage for its 2026 festive season, creating a warm-weather celebration rooted in the culture, food and landscapes of Lombok rather than imported holiday traditions.

Under the theme A Tale of Mandalika’s Golden Ages, the resort’s festive programming brings guests into contact with local artisans and fishermen while incorporating sea-to-table meals, fire-cooked feasts and communal gatherings beneath the stars. Guests can also extend the experience through the resort’s Destination Discoveries, with opportunities ranging from visits to South Sea pearl farms and sea turtle hatchling releases to snorkeling around the Gili Islands and trekking toward Mount Rinjani.

The festive program includes Christmas Eve and New Year’s Eve celebrations alongside curated family experiences and a New Year’s Eve DJ performance, giving travelers the opportunity to experience the holiday season through the lens of Lombok’s own culture and landscape.

The Curated Take: The most interesting part of a tropical Christmas is not simply trading snow for sunshine. It is finding a celebration that feels genuinely connected to where you are. By grounding its festive season in Sasak heritage, local craftsmanship, food traditions and the natural environment, The Sira offers a different model for holiday travel, one where the destination itself shapes the celebration.

item.title: Could This New Muscat Hotel Be Oman’s Next Luxury Address?
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Muscat is gaining a new luxury address with the opening of Tivoli LA VIE Muscat Hotel & Residences, a 79-room property that blends Tivoli’s European heritage with contemporary design and subtle references to Omani craftsmanship. Located within the prestigious LA VIE development in Madinat Al Irfan, the hotel places travelers near Muscat’s cultural and entertainment attractions while offering an experience designed around golf, gastronomy and wellbeing.

Guest rooms and suites feature natural textures, coastal tones, private balconies and views across the championship golf course, with details ranging from Amouage bath amenities to Dyson technology and Läderach chocolate at turndown. Dining is a major part of the property’s identity, from Mediterranean cuisine at S O L É to the rooftop SEEN by Olivier da Costa, the concept’s first Middle Eastern outpost. Nineteenth Sports Bar and Cigar Vault adds a more relaxed evening option, while Benihana and The Coffee Club are set to join the culinary lineup later this year.

Wellness is equally central, with Muscat’s first Anantara Spa, a rooftop infinity pool and Technogym fitness facilities. Golfers can play the Paul Thomas-designed 18-hole course or use the country’s only Toptracer facility. The property also positions itself for major events, with the 520-guest Juman Ballroom overlooking the golf course.

The Curated Take: Tivoli LA VIE is interesting not simply because it is new, but because of how deliberately it connects several facets of contemporary luxury travel in Oman. European hospitality, Omani design influences, serious golf, destination dining and a substantial wellness offering come together within a single address. For travelers looking beyond the region’s more established luxury destinations, the opening reflects Muscat’s growing ability to offer a sophisticated stay without losing its sense of place.

item.title: Entwined in the Swan Valley Celebrates Wine, Food and Heritage
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
The Swan Valley, one of Western Australia’s oldest wine regions, will welcome the return of Entwined in the Valley from October 5–18, 2026. The two-week celebration invites visitors to explore the region through a program of food, wine, heritage and hands-on experiences, with events ranging from long-table lunches among the vines to cellar-door visits, workshops and immersive masterclasses.

The festival offers a broad introduction to the Swan Valley’s culinary and agricultural character, combining behind-the-scenes tours and wine experiences with live entertainment and family-friendly activities. For travelers based in Perth, it provides an opportunity to venture into the nearby wine region, while those planning a longer Western Australian itinerary can use the event as a way to explore the area’s producers and historic landscapes.

The Curated Take:
Entwined is a reminder that wine regions are often best understood through more than tastings alone. By bringing together food, viticulture, heritage and participation, the festival gives visitors a fuller sense of the Swan Valley as a living agricultural and cultural landscape.

item.title: EMPIRE CROSSROADS
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
To eat in Marrakech is to taste the geography of conquest, exile, and endurance. Long before the city’s dusty ochre walls attracted luxury travelers and international chefs, its kitchens were quiet laboratories where distinct civilizational threads quietly braided together.

Moroccan cuisine is not a monolithic tradition; it is a layered archive. Sit at a table in the medina, and every dish reveals an origin story—from the ancient indigenous grains of the Atlas Mountains to the refined, aristocratic pastries brought by Andalusian refugees, to the fragrant spices carried across desert trade routes.

To truly understand the culinary soul of Marrakech, one must look beyond the conical lids of tagines and trace the historical currents that built its most iconic dishes.

The Amazigh Foundation: Tagine, Couscous, and the Clay Hearth

At the foundation of Moroccan food sits the Amazigh (Berber) people, the indigenous inhabitants of North Africa whose culinary identity is tethered directly to the soil and earth. Centuries before Arab, Ottoman, or European influences reached the interior, Amazigh cooks were mastering earthenware cooking over slow wood fires.

Two classic preparations define this ancient heritage:

The Tagine: Named after the iconic circular clay vessel with a tall, conical lid, the tagine is the heart of the Moroccan home. The cone acts as a natural condenser: as steam rises from braising lamb, chicken, or vegetables, it hits the cooler upper walls, condenses, and trickles back down. This closed-loop system allows tough meats to slow-cook into succulent stews with minimal water—a brilliant adaptation to an arid landscape.

Couscous: Hand-rolled from durum wheat semolina, authentic couscous is steamed multiple times in a perforated pot (kiskas) set over a simmering broth. Fluffed by hand between cycles, the light, airy grains absorb the essence of root vegetables, chickpeas, and aromatic broth. Topped with tfaya—a sweet crown of caramelized onions, raisins, and cinnamon—it represents the seamless harmony of indigenous rustic tradition and courtly refinement.

The Andalusian Exile: Pastilla’s Delicate Paradox

If the tagine and couscous represent the land, Pastilla (or B’stilla) represents the high art of the royal court. Its origins lie in 15th-century Al-Andalus (Moorish Spain). When Muslims and Jews were expelled during the Reconquista, they brought their sophisticated culinary techniques south into the imperial cities of Fez and Marrakech.

Pastilla is perhaps North Africa’s most complex gastronomic feat: a sweet and savory pie wrapped in paper-thin leaves of warqa pastry. Traditionally stuffed with slow-cooked pigeon (or tender shredded chicken), the filling is seasoned with saffron, ginger, nutmeg, and cinnamon, bound with whipped eggs, and layered with toasted, crushed almonds steeped in orange blossom water.

Dusted with powdered sugar and lattice lines of cinnamon, the first bite offers an intoxicating contrast—shattering pastry, warm aromatic fat, rich meat, and delicate floral sweetness. It is a living artifact of medieval Iberian court culture, preserved almost unchanged in Marrakech.

The Silk Road & Spice Routes: Harira and the Warmth of the Caravan

Marrakech’s historical position as a major trading hub between Sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East, and the Mediterranean made its markets an epicenter for exotic spice trading. Saffron from Taliouine, cumin from Alnif, and complex house blends like Ras el Hanout (”head of the shop”) became the invisible infrastructure of the city’s cooking.

This spice-route heritage culminates in Harira, a velvety, deeply comforting soup built on a base of tomatoes, chickpeas, lentils, and fine vermicelli. Infused with fresh cilantro, flat-leaf parsley, celery, and a warming blend of ginger and turmeric, Harira carries profound cultural weight during Ramadan, where it gently breaks the day’s fast alongside sweet medjool dates and honeyed chebakia pastries.

The Medina’s Local Invention: Tanjia Marrakchia

While the tagine is enjoyed across all of Morocco, Tanjia Marrakchia belongs exclusively to Marrakech. Born not in royal kitchens or family homes, but among the working-class male artisans and market vendors of the souks, Tanjia is a testament to urban ingenuity.

Unlike the shallow, wide tagine dish, a Tanjia is cooked in a tall, amphora-shaped clay urn. Cuts of beef shank or lamb are packed inside with garlic, cumin, saffron, smen (aged preserved butter), olive oil, and the sharp rind of preserved lemons.

The urn is sealed with paper, tied, and carried to the neighborhood farnatchi—the furnace room that heats the water for the local public bathhouse (hammam). There, buried in the smoldering ash pits for hours, the meat slow-braises in its own collagen and juices until melt-in-your-mouth tender.

Sanctuary at Four Seasons Resort Marrakech

After spending the day unraveling the sensory layers of the ancient medina, transitioning back to quiet luxury is part of the Marrakech rhythm. Set within 40 acres of secluded palm trees, quiet courtyards, and tranquil swimming pools, Four Seasons Resort Marrakech offers a peaceful retreat just moments from the historic city walls.

Here, culinary heritage is honored with refined elevated dining. Guests can savor expertly crafted tagines and regional specialties under the stars, or embark on curated culinary masterclasses with local chefs—learning the delicate balance of spices, preserved lemons, and slow-fire techniques that make Moroccan gastronomy world-renowned.

The Ritual of Connection: Atay and the Final Note

No meal in Marrakech ends abruptly; it dissolves into the slow, intentional ritual of Atay (Moroccan Mint Tea). Introduced via British trade ships in the 18th century, green gunpowder tea was quickly adapted by locals, who infused it with fresh spearmint leaves and generous blocks of sugar.

Poured from a high spout into small glass tumblers, the dramatic height aerates the hot liquid, forming a delicate crown of foam (regga) that locks in the fragrant mint oils while cooling the tea to drinking temperature.

To drink tea in Marrakech is to accept a historical contract of welcome. It serves as a gentle reminder that here, food is never just sustenance—it is a narrative passed down through centuries, waiting to be shared.

item.title: What If Chile’s Volcanic Landscape Became Your Spa?
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
In Chile’s Lake District, wellness is taking a distinctly geological turn. At Hotel AWA on the shores of Lake Llanquihue near Puerto Varas, a new Kayak & Soak experience pairs guided exploration of the Reloncaví Estuary with an exclusive soak in naturally heated pools at Termas de Cochamó, connecting two defining features of Los Lagos: its volcanic landscape and its thermal waters.

The approximately five-mile kayak journey takes about two hours before guests transition from the water to a private thermal pool surrounded by native vegetation for another two hours. Sea lions may make an appearance along the way, while the volcanic peaks of Osorno, Calbuco, Yates and Hornopirén provide the backdrop. The experience reflects AWA’s broader approach to travel, pairing active exploration with time to slow down and reconnect with the landscape.

The new experience also arrives as a contemporary thermal scene is emerging around the Reloncaví Estuary. At Termas del Sol, a series of thermal pools is connected by wooden walkways through native Patagonian forest, while new projects at Termas Botánicas in Ralún and Termas de Pichicolo are expanding the region’s geothermal offerings. Together, they are bringing a more design-conscious approach to Chile’s longstanding hot-springs tradition.

The Curated Take: What makes this story compelling is the way wellness is being tied directly to place. Rather than creating an artificial spa environment, AWA sends travelers into the volcanic landscape and then lets that same landscape provide the setting for restoration. It is a distinctly Chilean interpretation of wellness, where kayaking, wildlife, geology and thermal bathing become parts of one continuous experience.

item.title: What If You Could See the Northern Lights and Follow the Whales?
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Northern Norway offers a different kind of fall and winter escape, one shaped by seasonal wildlife, dramatic Arctic landscapes and experiences that are difficult to replicate elsewhere. From September through January, Up Norway’s six-day Autumnal Auroras & Wandering Whales journey connects the island of Senja with Tromsø, bringing travelers to a period when the Northern Lights return, migrating whales gather in the fjords and the landscape transitions from autumn into winter.

On Senja, one of Norway’s more dramatic and lesser-visited islands, travelers can follow the Norwegian Scenic Route, kayak along the coast and explore nearby national parks before retreating to a historic lighthouse or a sea-facing cabin with a private jacuzzi. Offshore, orcas and humpback whales follow enormous herring migrations into the fjords, with encounters taking place aboard Brim Explorer’s hybrid-electric catamaran for a quieter approach to wildlife watching. In Tromsø, the wilderness experience gives way to Arctic city life, with Northern Lights excursions paired with local food and culture, including a private boathouse dinner and a tasting menu at Restaurant Smak.

The Curated Take: The appeal of this journey is its timing. Rather than treating the Northern Lights as a standalone spectacle, the itinerary places them within a larger seasonal story, pairing the aurora with one of the Arctic’s great wildlife migrations. The combination of remote landscapes, locally rooted accommodations, responsible whale watching and Tromsø’s culinary scene creates a Northern Norway experience that feels immersive rather than simply checked off a winter bucket list.

Learn more about Up Norway’s Autumnal Auroras & Wandering Whales journey.

item.title: What If Your Jackson Hole Winter Escape Came With a Fireside Retreat?
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
In Jackson Hole, Wyoming, winter is as much about what happens after the adventure as it is about the snow itself. At the gateway to Grand Teton National Park, the 40-room Rusty Parrot Lodge & Spa offers a boutique base for experiencing the season, with world-class skiing, wildlife encounters, sleigh rides and the dramatic winter landscapes of the Tetons all close by.

Back at the lodge, the pace shifts from outdoor adventure to restorative comfort. Guests can unwind with treatments at Body Sage Spa, soak in the jacuzzi or settle in for seasonally inspired cuisine and fireside cocktails at the award-winning Wild Sage Restaurant & Bar. The intimate scale of the property keeps the experience distinctly personal, creating a retreat that feels connected to Jackson Hole rather than simply positioned within it.

The Curated Take: Jackson Hole has no shortage of luxury accommodations, but the appeal here is the balance between access and intimacy. Rusty Parrot makes the surrounding winter landscape the reason to venture out, then gives travelers a quieter, more indulgent place to return to. For travelers who want the full mountain experience without sacrificing a sense of retreat, that rhythm is part of the luxury.

item.title: What If Your Fall Foliage Escape Came With a Mountain Home of Your Own?
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
For travelers chasing peak fall color, the window can be short. Through late September and early October, InvitedHome’s luxury portfolio offers private mountain homes in Telluride, Aspen and Park City, putting travelers close to some of the West’s most spectacular autumn landscapes while replacing the traditional hotel stay with the privacy and space of a home.

In Telluride, Autumn Estate offers six bedrooms, expansive mountain views and multiple outdoor patios in the San Juan Mountains, with prime leaf-peeping dates from September 18 through 30. Aspen’s 24 Little Cloud Trail sits on a private 10-acre enclave at the base of Aspen Mountain, with views spanning Independence Pass, Red Mountain and the surrounding landscape. In Park City, Red Pine Estate provides six bedrooms, an outdoor hot tub, game room and private theater, with prime foliage dates extending from September 26 through October 6. Each property is particularly suited to families and multigenerational groups looking to gather between days spent exploring the changing landscape.

The Curated Take: There is something distinctly appealing about experiencing fall foliage from a private home rather than simply visiting it from a hotel. The luxury here is less about formality and more about having room to settle into the landscape, whether that means gathering around a long dinner, soaking in a hot tub after a day outdoors or simply watching the mountains change color from your own terrace. For multigenerational travel, the private-home model also makes the destination itself part of the experience.
